newsitem.title: UK: Major stares into abyss after UK by-election loss.
newsitem.headline: Major stares into abyss after UK by-election loss.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major conceded on Friday that his days in office were numbered unless he can stem the tide that swept the opposition Labour party to victory in a key by-election in northwest England.
Labour candidate Ben Chapman overturned a Conservative majority of 8,183 votes to win the affluent commuter-belt constituency of Wirral South by a margin of 7,888 votes.
Major vowed to recapture the seat at the general election, which he is expected to hold on May 1.
But he admitted to a television interviewer: "If opinion does not change then we are going to have a Labour government."
It was the first time that Major has openly contemplated the prospect that his ruling Conservative party, in power since 1979, might not win its fifth consecutive term of office.
However Major, who came from behind to win the 1992 election, made it clear he would not go down without a fight.
Declaring that the "phoney war" was over, he foreshadowed a bitter general election campaign by warning voters that Labour was planning an early tax-raising budget.

"The battle is still to be fought. Does Britain change course, does it move towards the policies of socialism? Or does it stay with the policies that have made it successful? That is the choice that lies ahead," Major said.
If the Wirral South result, which was broadly in line with national opinion polls, was repeated at the general election, Labour would win by a landslide.
Chapman polled 53 percent of the vote as Labour enjoyed a 17 percent swing -- dwarfing the 4.3 percent swing it would need to win the general election. Turnout was a high 73 percent.

Labour leader Tony Blair said the result in Wirral South -- a middle-class seat that has always returned a Conservative -- showed that the party he has steered to the centre-ground of British politics was now widely trusted and ready for power.
"Many of the people who live there have never put their trust in Labour before, but yesterday they did," he told the Welsh Labour party conference in Llandudno.
"The result is nothing short of a political uprising against the Tories deep in their heartland. There are no no-go areas for New Labour," Blair said.
The defeat puts Major in a minority in parliament of 322 seats compared with 323 for the combined opposition.
Labour accepts it has little chance of triggering an early election because Major has the support of nine Protestant Ulster Unionist members of parliament from Northern Ireland.
Nevertheless, Blair told Major to "stop dithering" and set the date for the election instead of clinging on to power by his fingertips.

Labour officials noted that no party had clawed back a deficit of the size the Conservatives now face in the two months that probably remain before the general election. Two polls this week put Labour's national lead at 20-21 percentage points.
Pro-Conservative newspapers added to the ruling party's gloom. "The spectre of a general election defeat was haunting John Major today," The Express said in its lead report.
"We have never treated any general election as being sewn up. We've lost four elections," Labour's deputy leader, John Prescott, said. "But we now think there is the best chance we have ever had."

But Major, who is always at his best when his back is against the wall, still believes that residual fear of Labour will outweigh the message sent by Wirral South voters that it is time for a change after 18 years of rule by the same party.

"The people of Wirral have two shots. They have used their first shot to give us a kick up the backside. It didn't change the face of Britain, but a second effort would change the face of Britain," Home Secretary Michale Howard, the interior minister, said. "The Tory fight back starts here." REUTER
